destination.title: Can Your School Punish You for a Post You Made Off Campus?

short11: A post you made on the weekend, from home.
Can your school punish you for it?
A fourteen-year-old didn't make the varsity cheer team, and vented on Snapchat, a post meant to disappear.
A screenshot reached the coach, and the school suspended her from cheer for a year.
In 2021, the Supreme Court ruled eight to one: schools usually can't punish ordinary off-campus speech.
The line between home and school was redrawn.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: A famous 1969 case said so: young people do not "shed their constitutional rights at the schoolhouse gate" .

In 2021, a fourteen-year-old's disappearing Snapchat reached the Supreme Court of the United States, and the answer it gave shapes the rights of every student — and every parent — in the age of the phone .
In 2017 she is fourteen, a student at Mahanoy Area High School in Pennsylvania, and a cheerleader — on the junior varsity squad .
To understand the stakes, you have to go back to that 1969 case, Tinker v.
Those students had worn the armbands in 1965 to mourn the dead of the Vietnam War, after the school banned that specific protest in advance.
Follow it far enough, and a student never really leaves school at all.
In 2021, the Supreme Court ruled for Brandi Levy.
It pointedly did not say that schools can never reach off-campus speech.
But it points at the real difficulty: nobody, including the Court, drew a clean line — because in the age of the phone, a clean line may not exist.

shorts.angle: The school's entire case rested on disruption, and the disruption turned out to be a few minutes of talk in one class, which is why Breyer answered with a line about what schools are for.
shorts.type: C — a quotation from the opinion
shorts.avoids: The existing Short gives the outcome and the exception for threats and bullying. It never gives the Court's reasoning, the actual size of the disruption the school claimed, or the sentence the ruling turns on.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: The one justice who dissented, and the history he said the majority was discarding.

lines.text: The school said the post disrupted the school. Here is what that disruption was.
source_lines: The Court also looked at what had actually happened, and found almost nothing.

lines.text: A few minutes of discussion in one class. That is all. The school had punished frustration, not chaos.
source_lines: Brandi's post had caused, at most, a few minutes of discussion in one class.
The school had punished frustration, not chaos.

lines.text: Justice Stephen Breyer wrote the opinion. A school's authority over what students say, he explained, is weaker off campus than on. There, a student is in the care of her parents.
source_lines: Justice Stephen Breyer wrote the opinion, and his reasoning was careful. A school's special authority over what students say, he explained, is weaker off campus than on. Off campus, a student is normally in the care of her parents, not the school.

lines.text: Then came the line the ruling turns on. America's public schools, he wrote, are the nurseries of democracy. The place a free society teaches the next generation to tolerate the speech it dislikes. A school that punishes every unpopular word teaches the opposite.
source_lines: America's public schools, he wrote, are the "nurseries of democracy" — the place a free society teaches the next generation to tolerate the speech it dislikes. A school that punishes every unpopular off-campus word does not model that lesson; it teaches the opposite.

lines.text: Everything the school did rested on one word, and it is worth knowing what that word was actually covering.

shorts.angle: The Court protected the student and then deliberately refused to say where the line is, leaving every student and parent in a gray zone decided one post at a time.
shorts.type: A — second-person threat ('this can reach you')
shorts.avoids: The existing Short states the eight to one outcome and names threats and bullying as exceptions. It does not say the Court refused on purpose to draw a bright line, or that the speech it protected was petty by design.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: The 1969 case that set the old test, and why the phone made that test stop working.
shorts.loop_join: L5 says the vagueness was chosen, so L1 returns as a deliberate decision rather than a gap the Court forgot to close.

lines.text: The Court protected the student and refused to tell you where the line is.
source_lines: It pointedly did not say that schools can never reach off-campus speech.

lines.text: It pointedly did not say that schools can never reach off campus speech. It listed what might still justify stepping in. Serious bullying or harassment. Threats. Cheating.
source_lines: It pointedly did not say that schools can never reach off-campus speech.
It listed the kinds of things that might still justify a school stepping in, even off campus: serious bullying or harassment aimed at other students, threats, cheating, breaking real rules.

lines.text: Then it declined to draw one bright line. The result is a gray zone every student and parent now lives in, decided post by post.
source_lines: It declined to draw one bright line, leaving the hard cases for later
The result is a gray zone that every student and parent now lives in, decided post by post, case by case.

lines.text: And notice what the Court protected. Not a noble political statement. A crude, throwaway post that vanished in seconds. On purpose. Free speech is tested by the speech we find petty.
source_lines: And notice what the Court actually protected. Not a noble political statement, but a crude, throwaway Snapchat that vanished in seconds. That was on purpose.
free speech is tested not by the speech we admire, but by the speech we find petty, or rude, or pointless

lines.text: So the gray zone is not an accident. It is what eight justices decided they could live with.
